      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The <span class="qt0">stomach</span> is an organ between the esophagus and the small intestine. It mixes food with <span class="qt0">stomach</span> acid and helps digest protein. <span class="qt0">Stomach</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> mostly affects older people - two-thirds of people who have it are over age 65. Your risk of getting it is also higher if you:</p><ul><li>Have had a Helicobacter pylori infection</li><li>Have had <span class="qt0">stomach</span> inflammation</li><li>Are a man</li><li>Eat lots of  salted, smoked, or pickled foods </li><li>Smoke cigarettes </li><li>Have a family history of <span class="qt0">stomach</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span></li></ul><p>It is hard to diagnose <span class="qt0">stomach</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> in its early stages. Indigestion and <span class="qt0">stomach</span> discomfort can be symptoms of early <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, but other problems can cause the same symptoms. In advanced cases, there may be blood in your stool, vomiting, unexplained weight loss, jaundice, or trouble swallowing. Doctors diagnose <span class="qt0">stomach</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> with a physical exam, blood and imaging tests, an endoscopy, and a biopsy.</p><p>Because it is often found late, it can be hard to treat <span class="qt0">stomach</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.  Treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation or a combination.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/helicobacterpyloriinfections.html">
      <content name="title">Helicobacter pylori Infections</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">H. pylori Infections</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a type of bacteria that causes infection in the <span class="qt0">stomach</span>. It is the main cause of peptic ulcers, and it can also cause gastritis and <span class="qt0">stomach</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>About 30 to 40% of people in the United States get an H. pylori infection. Most people get it as a child. H. pylori usually does not cause symptoms. But it can break down the inner protective coating in some people's <span class="qt0">stomachs</span> and cause inflammation. This can lead to gastritis or a peptic ulcer.</p><p>Researchers aren't sure how H. pylori spreads. They think that it may spread by unclean food and water, or through contact with an infected person's saliva and other body fluids.</p><p>A peptic ulcer causes a dull or burning pain in your <span class="qt0">stomach</span>, especially when you have an empty <span class="qt0">stomach</span>. It lasts for minutes to hours, and it may come and go for several days or weeks.  It may also cause other symptoms, such as bloating, nausea, and weight loss. If you have the symptoms of a peptic ulcer, your health care provider will check to see whether you have H. pylori.  There are blood, breath, and stool tests to check for H. pylori. In some cases, you may need an upper endoscopy, often with a biopsy.</p><p>If you do have a peptic ulcer, the treatment is with a combination of antibiotics and acid-reducing medicines. You will need to be tested again after treatment to make sure the infection is gone.</p><p>There is no vaccine for H. pylori. Since H. pylori might spread through unclean food and water, you might be able to prevent it if you:</p><ul><li>Wash your hands after using the bathroom and before eating</li><li>Eat properly prepared food</li><li>Drink water from a clean, safe source</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/esophagealcancer.html">
      <content name="title">Esophageal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The esophagus is a hollow tube that carries food and liquids from your throat to your <span class="qt0">stomach</span>.  Early esophageal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> usually does not cause symptoms. Later, you may have symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>Painful or difficult swallowing</li><li>Weight loss</li><li>A hoarse voice or cough that doesn't go away</li></ul><p>You're at greater risk for getting esophageal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> if you smoke, drink heavily, or have acid reflux. Your risk also goes up as you age</p><p> Your doctor uses imaging tests and a biopsy to diagnose esophageal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.  Treatments include surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy.  You might also need nutritional support, since the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> or treatment may make it hard to swallow.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/benefitsofexercise.html">
      <content name="title">Benefits of Exercise</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Exercise Benefits</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>We have heard it many times before -- regular exercise is good for you, and it can help you manage your weight. But if you are like many people, you are busy, you sit most of the day at your job, and you haven't yet changed your exercise habits. The good news is that it's never too late to start. You can start slowly and find ways to fit more physical activity into your life. To get the most benefit, you should try to get the recommended amount of physical activity for your age. If you can do that, the payoff is that you will feel better, may help prevent or control many diseases, and will likely even live longer.</p>What are the health benefits of exercise?<p>Regular exercise and physical activity may:</p><ul><li>Help you get to and stay at a healthy weight. Along with diet, exercise plays an important role in maintaining a healthy weight and preventing obesity. If you are at a healthy weight, you can maintain it if the calories you eat and drink are equal to the amount of energy you burn. To lose weight, you need to use more calories than you eat and drink.</li><li>Reduce your risk of heart diseases. Exercise strengthens your heart and improves your circulation. The increased blood flow raises the oxygen levels in your body. This helps lower your risk of heart diseases such as coronary artery disease and heart attack. Regular exercise can also lower high blood pressure, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels, all of which are risk factors for heart disease.</li><li>Help your body manage blood glucose (blood sugar) and insulin levels. Exercise can lower your blood glucose levels and help your insulin work better. This can reduce your risk of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes. And if you already have one of these diseases, exercise can help you manage it.</li><li>Help you manage a chronic health condition. For example, regular physical activity may help reduce pain and improve function in adults with arthritis. It can also help support daily living activities for people with disabilities. This may help them be more independent.</li><li>Help you quit smoking. Exercise may make it easier to quit smoking by reducing your cravings and withdrawal symptoms. It can also help limit the weight you might gain when you stop smoking.</li><li>Improve your mental health and mood. During exercise, your body releases chemicals that can improve your mood and make you feel more relaxed. This can help you deal with stress, manage anxiety, and reduce your risk of depression.</li><li>Help keep your thinking, learning, and judgment skills sharp as you age. Exercise stimulates your body to release proteins and other chemicals that improve the structure and function of your brain.</li><li>Strengthen your bones and muscles. Regular exercise can help kids and teens build strong bones. Later in life, it can also slow the loss of bone density that comes with age. Doing muscle-strengthening activities can help you increase or maintain your muscle mass and strength. For older adults, this can mean staying independent, like being able to get in and out of a chair or bed without help.</li><li>Reduce your risk of some <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>, including colon, breast, uterine, bladder, esophageal, kidney, <span class="qt0">stomach</span>, and lung <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. There are different ways that physical activity may lower the risk of these <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>. For example, it can strengthen your immune system and reduce inflammation in your body. It also helps prevent obesity, which is a risk factor for many <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>.</li><li>Reduce your risk of falls. For older adults, doing balance and muscle-strengthening activities can help reduce your risk of falling.</li><li>Improve your sleep. Exercise can help you fall asleep faster and stay asleep longer.</li><li>Boost your energy. Exercise helps your heart and lungs work better, which can leave you feeling more energetic throughout the day.</li><li>Improve your sexual health. Regular exercise may lower the risk of erectile dysfunction (ED) in men. For those who already have ED, exercise may help improve their sexual function. In women, exercise may increase sexual arousal.</li><li>Increase your chances of living longer. Studies show that physical activity can reduce your risk of dying early from the leading causes of death, like heart disease and certain <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>.</li></ul>How can I make exercise a part of my regular routine?<p>Here are some tips to help you make exercise part of your daily routine:</p><ul><li>Make everyday activities more active. Even small changes can help. You can take the stairs instead of the elevator. Walk down the hall to a coworker's office instead of sending an email. Wash the car yourself. Park further away from your destination.</li><li>Be active with friends and family. Having a workout partner may make you more likely to enjoy exercise. You can also plan social activities that involve exercise. Consider joining an exercise group or class, such as a dance class, hiking club, or volleyball team.</li><li>Keep track of your progress. Keeping a log of your activity or using a fitness tracker may help you set goals and stay motivated.</li><li>Make exercise more fun. Try listening to music or watching TV while you exercise. Also, mix things up a little bit - if you stick with just one type of exercise, you might get bored. Try doing a combination of activities.</li><li>Find activities that you can do even when the weather is bad. You can walk in a mall, climb stairs, or work out in a gym even if the weather stops you from exercising outside.</li><li>Remember that some physical activity is better than none.  Do what you can! Even 5 minutes of physical activity has real health benefits.</li></ul></content>

      <content name="altTitle">Gastrointestinal Stromal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Tumors</span></span></content>

      <content name="altTitle">Jejunal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your small intestine is part of your digestive system.  It is a long tube that connects your <span class="qt0">stomach</span> to your large intestine. Intestinal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is rare, but eating a high-fat diet or having Crohn's disease, celiac disease, or a history of  colonic polyps can increase your risk.</p><p>Possible signs of small intestine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> include:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Abdominal</span> pain</li><li>Weight loss for no reason</li><li>Blood in the stool</li><li>A lump in the <span class="qt0">abdomen</span></li></ul><p>Imaging tests that create pictures of the small intestine and the area around it can help diagnose intestinal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> and show whether it has spread.</p><p>Surgery is the most common treatment. Additional options include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or a combination.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>
